response.passage: In a local market, a shopkeeper organizes his stock of sweets. He has two types of boxes: one containing 12 pieces and another containing 18 pieces. To ensure he has equal stacks of each, he calculates the Least Common Multiple (LCM) of 12 and 18. He writes 12 as 2 squared times 3, and 18 as 2 times 3 squared. By taking the highest power of each prime factor present, he finds the LCM is 36. He also notes that the Highest Common Factor (HCF) is 6, obtained by taking the lowest power of common prime factors. He reminds his assistant that while the product of two numbers equals the product of their HCF and LCM, this rule does not apply to three different types of boxes. Later, a customer asks if the ratio of the box dimensions, which is 22 divided by 7, makes the value irrational. The shopkeeper explains that 22/7 is a rational approximation, but the true value of pi is indeed irrational. Finally, he checks a new batch of 4 raised to the power n sweets, noting that since 4 only contains the prime factor 2, it can never end in the digit 0, regardless of the value of n.
response.summary: The shopkeeper uses prime factorisation to manage his sweet inventory and determine stack sizes. He correctly distinguishes between rational approximations and irrational numbers while applying rules for HCF and LCM.
